## Comparing the CNN and Siamese results

<!-- Task 6: which digits carry more writer information; how session changes affect performance. -->
The Siamese network and CNN were employed on different tasks; SNN for writer verification and CNN for writer identification, respectively. Their accuracy metrics are not directly comparable. Nevertheless, both tuned models substantially outperformed what would be expected by chance: SNN achieved a test balanced accuracy of `r snn_hpo_test_results` (compared with 50% baseline for binary verification of same- vs different-writer) and the CNN a test accuracy of `r cnn_hpo_pct(cnn_hpo_test_accuracy)` (compared with a 5% baseline for classifying one out of 20 writers). These results indicate that both networks learned useful writer-related features for their respective tasks.

```{r extract-test-results}
cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy <- cnn_hpo_test |>
  group_by(digit) |>
  summarise(accuracy = 100 * mean(person_id == predicted),
            .groups = "drop")

cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_lowest <- cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy %>% slice_min(accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_highest <- cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy %>% slice_max(accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

snn_digit_accuracy <- snn_hpo_test_results_table_digits %>%
  filter(Digit != "All digits") %>%
  mutate(Balanced_accuracy = 100 * Balanced_accuracy)

snn_digit_accuracy_lowest <- snn_digit_accuracy %>%
  slice_min(Balanced_accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

snn_digit_accuracy_highest <- snn_digit_accuracy %>%
  slice_max(Balanced_accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

At the digit level, the networks had varied performance. The tuned CNN's identification accuracy ranged from `r round(cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_lowest$accuracy,1)`% for digit `r cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_lowest$digit` to `r round(cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_highest$accuracy,1)`% for digit `r cnn_hpo_test_digit_accuracy_highest$digit` (@cnn_hpo_test_digit). In comparison, the tuned SNN's balanced accuracy ranged from `r round(snn_digit_accuracy_lowest$Balanced_accuracy, 1)` for digit `r snn_digit_accuracy_lowest$Digit` % to `r round(snn_digit_accuracy_highest$Balanced_accuracy, 1)`% for digit `r snn_digit_accuracy_highest$Digit` (@snn_test_results_table_digits). Notably, digit 2 had the highest identification accuracy for the CNN but the lowest balanced accuracy for the SNN.

Although the results may initially appear contradictory, they suggest that the usefulness of a digit depends on the nature of the task being performed. Digits achieving a high identification accuracy (CNN) and low balanced accuracy (SNN) (e.g., digit '2') means that 2 can help to distinguish among the writers represented in the training data, but that the same digit does not provide equally useful information in verifying whether two samples were written by the same writer
Conversely, digits with high balanced accuracy (SNN) and low accuracy (CNN) may provide useful evidence for distinguishing same-writer from different-writer pairs, without being sufficiently distinctive to identify a particular writer from the 20 known writers. For example, digit 0 may exhibit this pattern, while digits 3 and 4 achieved mid-to-high performance across both metrics which may show that it serves usefulness in both tasks. However, it is important to note that these interpretations are suggestive rather than definitive, as these models were evaluated using different data splits and under different generalisation settings. 

```{r extract-session-accuracy-results}
session_accuracy <- snn_hpo_test_results_table_sessions %>%
  filter(Session != "All sessions") %>%
  mutate(Balanced_accuracy = 100 * Balanced_accuracy)

same_session <- session_accuracy %>%
  filter(Session == "Same session")

different_session <- session_accuracy %>%
  filter(Session == "Different session")
```


Session-related performance was assessed using the SNN, by comparing performance for pairs drawn from the same sessions with pairs from different sessions. This was not possible for the CNN, because its session-level split was designed to perform writer identification on held-out sessions. The SNN achieved higher balanced accuracy for same-session pairs than for different-session pairs (`r round(same_session$Balanced_accuracy,1)`% versus `r round(different_session$Balanced_accuracy,1)`%). This result is consistent with our expectation that writer variation across sessions makes verification more difficult. However, this difference alone does not establish which sources of variation were responsible (e.g., natural writer variation, different writing materials).

Performance also varied considerably across writers in the CNN evaluation. The model identified writers 7 & 18 with near-perfect accuracy, whereas it nearly always misclassified samples from writers 5 & 13. This suggests that some writers had handwriting that was far more distinguishable than the others. Because the SNN datasets were split by writer, we cannot compare the performance with respect to individual writers as directly, although we note that writers 5 & 13 happened to be in the validation set used for HP tuning, which may explain why validation accuracy was lower than test accuracy (`r round(threshold_scores[best_index]*100, 2)`% versus `r  100 * snn_hpo_test_results`. The higher test result may reflect differences in the difficulty of the validation and test writers, as well as sampling variability, rather than a general improvement in performance on unseen writers.

Finally, hyperparameter tuning indicated moderate sensitivity for both models to the learning rate. For the CNN, tuning the other hyperparameters offered no substantial additional improvements in performance, whereas a smaller batch size tended to improve the SNN's balanced accuracy. Overall, the results demonstrate both networks can learn useful features from handwritten images for writer identification and writer verification, while also highlighting the effects of digit choice, session variation, writer-specific differences, and evaluation design on measured performance.
